episode_title: Supply and Demand: Paxos on What Moves Stablecoins Into Corporate Treasury

real_qa.q: Why did Paxos obtain a New York trust company license in 2015 when most other stablecoin companies were operating without regulatory oversight?
real_qa.r: Paxos was founded in 2012 and became the first company to get a New York trust company license back in 2015, then converted that to an OCC national trust company in December of last year. Walter Hesert explains that Paxos set up the business to operate out of highly regulated entities because they believed in mass adoption of the technology and wanted to work with the most trusted and discerning firms in the world. Being regulated like a bank from the outset, with prudential oversight from regulators, was ahead of its time but differentiated Paxos when working with major financial institutions.
real_qa.requete: Paxos New York trust company license 2015

real_qa.q: What was Paxos's role in the PayPal Bitcoin and Ethereum trading launch in October 2020?
real_qa.r: Less than a year after Walter Hesert and Paul Bancis first met in October 2019 at Money 2020 in Vegas, Paxos went live on PayPal as the infrastructure provider for the trading use case of buying Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies on the PayPal platform. Paxos provided both the trading engine and the wallet infrastructure for this launch, which was a significant achievement in 2019.

real_qa.q: How does Paxos's regulatory approach compare to Circle and Tether in the stablecoin market?
real_qa.r: The three largest stablecoin issuers are Tether (least regulated, explicitly avoiding regulatory oversight), Circle (partnered with Visa, BlackRock, and BNY but without prudential regulatory oversight of USDC issuance), and Paxos (regulated like a bank with prudential oversight since its first stablecoin issuance in 2018). Paxos subjects itself to oversight not just on consumer-facing activities but on every aspect of stablecoin issuance, while Tether is unregulated and Circle lacks regulatory oversight despite trust-building partnerships.

real_qa.q: What is Paxos's current wallet infrastructure reach and customer base?
real_qa.r: Paxos powers over 20 million active wallets for companies like PayPal, Venmo, and large financial institutions like Charles Schwab. This wallet infrastructure represents one major product line alongside the tokenization side where Paxos takes assets and tokenizes them onto the blockchain across various asset classes.

real_qa.q: How did the GENIUS Act affect Paxos's business and infrastructure development?
real_qa.r: The GENIUS Act created a regulatory framework that defines stablecoins as payment instruments, providing market clarity. Since GENIUS passed, Paxos is busier than ever, working with dozens of large financial institutions including multiple GSIBs on new stablecoin infrastructure. The regulatory clarity from GENIUS has resulted in multiples more infrastructure being laid than would otherwise have occurred.

real_qa.q: Why did Paxos's stablecoin issuance drop from $25 billion to a lower level in the past?
real_qa.r: Paxos had $25 billion of stablecoin issuance at one point, but regulators shut it down as a direct result of how Paxos subjected itself to regulatory oversight, including prudential oversight from the DOJ and New York Fed. This regulatory constraint was a trade-off for pursuing a highly regulated business model.

guest.bio_context: Walter Hesert joined Paxos approximately nine years ago after spending about a decade building technology and businesses in highly regulated, transactional spaces, including building software for the global pari-mutual horse betting industry. At Paxos, he has held multiple roles and currently oversees go-to-market teams (revenue, solutions, marketing, and communications) as well as the global policy function. He was instrumental in the 2019 PayPal partnership at Money 2020 in Vegas, which led to the launch of Bitcoin and Ethereum trading on PayPal with Paxos providing infrastructure.
